summary: LUNAR NAV is a data driven Mission Control dashboard built to help mission planners, educators, and students evaluate lunar south pole landing sites for Artemis IV. Created using Python, Streamlit, Plotly, and a SQLite database, LUNAR NAV brings together real NASA ephemeris and topography data, including LOLA elevation models and LRO illumination datasets, to simulate surface conditions across the lunar cycle. Users can scrub through a lunar day progression timeline spanning 0 to 29.5 Earth days to track real time solar and Earth elevation angles, check surface illumination percentages, and analyse terrain horizons. By combining high resolution orbital mapping with reliable scientific telemetry, LUNAR NAV makes complex planetary datasets easy to explore and understand.
details:
• What it does and how it works: LUNAR NAV is an interactive web-based Lunar Landing Site Navigator designed to help users explore high-priority lunar south pole landing regions including the Haworth Crater. It features an orbital map connected to a timeline slider representing a full 29.5 day lunar cycle. As you move through the timeline, the app pulls data from a local database built  by collecting custom CSV files, created utilising NASA data sources, allowing it to calculate corresponding Solar & Earth elevation angles and sunlight exposure percentages. Users can also select a variety of candidate locations to see detailed mission profiles and charts showing Earth and Sun visibility from a particular site across the lunar cycle.
    • Languages and Core Frameworks: Python, HTML, and CSS.
    • Data and Backend: SQLite, pandas, and spiceypy were used to generate and manipulate custom CSV files generated from NASA data.
    • Visualisation and UI: Figma, Streamlit, Plotly for interactive maps and charts, and PIL for image handling. The dashboard utilises Plotly for all data visualisations and maps, providing powerful interactive tools that make exploring planetary data seamless. Because the charts are fully dynamic, you can easily zoom in and out, focus on a specific section of the lunar cycle or map area, and pan across axes to inspect fine telemetry details. Users can also hover over data points for exact readings and use the integrated toolbar to export graphs as high quality images straight to their device for reports or presentations.
    • Development and Deployment: VS Code, Git version control, and Streamlit Community Cloud.
    • Artificial Intelligence: Used for research support, code troubleshooting, and structuring assistance. ChatGPT was used to help create the CSV files and Google Gemini was used to help guide the development of the project.
  • Creativity and engineering considerations: When implementing the app online, we encountered pathing issues in large database files. To mend this, we programmed the app to construct a database as it boots, by extracting data from custom CSV files, ensuring it runs smoothly and consistently. Visually, the app uses a clean high-contrast dark mode aesthetic with custom text formatting to coherently convey information. For the sake of submission, placeholder values have been used for all landing sites excluding HW10, which has a detailed, accurate description for demonstration purposes.
  • Limitations: The current software has some technical limitations. Terrain elevation for the horizon is currently measured at 10m outward intervals for only 10km, and at 2-degree intervals from the azimuth. This means smaller land features are not accounted for when mapping the horizon.
  • Future roadmap and what we ran out of time for: Due to hackathon time constraints, we were unable to implement planned features including an automated mission viability scoring and dynamic surface temperature calculations based on time and sunlight exposure. However, these are planned as key features for future updates, alongside dynamic shadow mapping throughout a lunar cycle to provide an even more immersive mission control experience.
